context: mega process plant · potlines and their power supply; pots are started one by one over months

brief.intro: New to this project type? An aluminium smelter makes metal by passing a very large electric current through alumina dissolved in a molten bath, in hundreds of identical steel cells called pots, connected in series in a building a kilometre long — the potline. Carbon anodes, made in the smelter's own carbon plant, are consumed and replaced continuously; the liquid metal is tapped and cast into ingots or billets in the casthouse. The smelter uses as much electricity as a city, so it comes with a rectifier substation and usually its own power plant or a dedicated grid connection. Construction is highly repetitive — pot shells, linings and busbars many hundreds of times — and the plant does not switch on: pots are energised a few at a time, so start-up itself lasts months.

must_get_right: Power first: the rectifier substation and the power supply must be ready before any pot can start, and power contracts drive the start-up curve.
The carbon plant has to produce good anodes before the first pot starts — it is commissioned months ahead of the potline.
Potline work is mass repetition; plan it as production lines (shells per week, linings per week, busbar welds per day) section by section.
Start-up is a schedule of its own: pots are energised a few per day for months. First metal is a milestone, not the finish.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by plant area along the process line and by discipline, with every long-lead machine tracked from order to factory test, shipping and arrival.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Standard site calendar with extended shifts on the potline production lines; pot start-up runs continuously, around the clock.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Site, piling and potroom buildings → pot shells → lining → busbar → superstructures, section by section. In parallel: carbon plant to first anodes; rectifier substation to energisation; gas treatment and alumina handling; casthouse. Then potline energised → pots started in sequence → first metal → full line. The critical path runs through the power supply and rectifiers or the carbon plant.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The process technology and vendor are fixed before design starts; vendor drawings for foundations arrive on the agreed dates; permanent power and water are available before cold commissioning; raw material for trial production is on site.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy machines need crane access and often must enter before the cladding or a wall is closed. Vendor supervisors are booked for fixed periods. Clean, dry, powered conditions are required before precision equipment is unpacked.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: power-supply readiness, rectifier delivery, anode quality at start-up, busbar welding productivity, and pot failures during early operation. Contingency is held before first metal.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by plant area and discipline; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the installation crews and the vendor supervisors — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
